data.description:
Spine task 1 of D1 v1. Produce docs/engineering/01-stack-decision.md: the framework/stack decision for the product app, in the form the front-end design plan (docs/design/00-frontend-design-plan.md) section 4 Phase C requires — options considered, criteria, a recommendation, and what would reverse it. Nothing else in the D1 build starts until this lands; every other v1 task depends on it transitively.

IMPLEMENTS: docs/engineering/00-d1-v1-milestone-plan.md section 3 row C-01 (IN by mandate — front-end design plan section 4 Phase C). Section 8.3 names it as spine task 1.

DECISION CONTEXT. The criteria are already fixed and are not re-derived here. The stack must be: (a) implementable by agent ICs working from text alone; (b) runnable under docker compose (infra rule, CLAUDE.md); (c) testable with NO external accounts — the right-sizing rule in milestone plan section 8.2 requires every task to name a verification method that works with the accounts we actually have, which is currently none; (d) free of paid services or licences; (e) able to keep every Stripe call behind a single enforceable chokepoint (the custody guard, the next spine task — see assumption A3, milestone plan section 5); (f) deployable to Digital Ocean when the deployment milestone opens (out of v1, but do not choose something that forecloses it); (g) able to consume the AS-29 design tokens (docs/design/tokens/tokens.css) without a build-step fight (front-end design plan section 5).

Our internal-tooling convention (zero dependencies, node --test, compose per app — see apps/chat/package.json) is EVIDENCE for this decision, not the decision. A product with a payment integration and real users may justify different answers; that is what this task is for. AS-31 named the slot and the criteria and deliberately named no candidates, because choosing a stack inside a scoping task is deciding in the wrong order.

VERIFICATION: the doc exists, names at least two real options, evaluates each against all seven criteria above, states a recommendation and the conditions that would reverse it. QA checks that every criterion is addressed for every option — this is a decision record, not a preference. Runnable now; no accounts, no code.

NOT IN THIS TASK: writing any application code (that is the scaffold task); choosing a hosting provider (Digital Ocean is already the infra rule); choosing a database engine beyond what the stack decision implies — if the stack leaves it open, say so and leave it to the data-model task.
data.title: D1 v1: stack decision for the product app (options, criteria, recommendation)

data.body:
SEQUENCING VERDICT: PROCEED. This task was flagged because two documents I authored on the same day disagree. docs/design/00-frontend-design-plan.md Phase C says the stack decision comes AFTER Phase B exists ('deciding a stack before the flows and the product are fixed is deciding in the wrong order'). The AS-31 plan and milestone plan section 8.3 make it spine task 1, ahead of AS-30. AS-30 has not run, so under Phase C's literal rule this task should not be starting. Resolved in the plan file section 2, not silently.

WHY PROCEED, shortest form: Phase C gave a rule ('after Phase B') and, in the same sentence, the REASON for the rule ('before the flows and the product are fixed'). The rule was a proxy for the condition. They coincided when written, because the product itself was still open. They have since come apart: the board fixed the product (step-5, 08-board-decision.md), and the milestone plan — which did not exist when Phase C was written — fixed the capability set (24 IN rows), the exact 7 screens and their routes, and a boundary filter that FORBIDS the surface growing, with 2 screens of headroom frozen. Phase B adds layout and states ledgers: depth on a fixed surface, not new surface.

Three supporting facts. (1) AS-36 and AS-30 are mutually independent and this is already on record in both directions — AS-30's own description says 'no framework/stack commitment is implied by this task', and its deliverable is framework-neutral static HTML. AS-30 is backlog with AS-29 done, i.e. pullable right now; proceeding delays it by zero. (2) Of the seven criteria, wireframes bear materially on at most one — (a) implementable-from-text, via the interactivity envelope — and that envelope is bounded by the capability table (no IN row for real-time state, offline, drag-drop, rich text, canvas or charts) rather than by wireframes. Criterion (g) is settled by a DELIVERED artifact: tokens.css states 'no build step, safe to link directly'. (3) Applied literally today, Phase C's rule INVERTS section 4.4 of its own document: AS-36 gates AS-37 which gates the whole server fan, so gating AS-36 on wireframes puts every non-UI task in v1 behind a design deliverable nothing else waits on — the exact failure the ready-queue invariant was built to prevent.

I am the author of both documents and therefore the party most tempted to rule the newer one right. Plan section 2.3 states the blocking steelman at full strength and answers it not with confidence but with a mechanism: the residual risk becomes reversal trigger T1 (observable, threshold, priced action), and separability of the front-end choice from the server choice is promoted to criterion (h) so a wrong front-end call costs the four UI tasks and never the server fan. Taking the objection seriously is what produced (h).

NOT CLAIMED: that Phase C was wrong when written. It was right — on 2026-08-31 morning the product was genuinely undecided and D1/C2/D4 are different technical shapes. Its error is narrower: it stated a proxy where it meant a condition, and the world moved.

AMENDMENT: docs/design/00-frontend-design-plan.md Phase C is the losing document and is amended in the implementation tick, wording given verbatim in plan section 3. docs/ is engineering-owned and I authored the file; NO top-level markdown needs changing (checked — README's only mention is a directory-map row that stays true), and employees never edit those anyway. The original sentence is preserved in quotation inside the amendment rather than deleted: records here are amended in the open. Acceptance criterion 10 checks the amendment landed, because without it the repo holds two contradictory sequencing rules and the next agent gets to pick which to obey.

WHAT THE PLAN SETTLES: criteria as GATES (compose, tests with no accounts AND no network egress, $0, enforceable Stripe chokepoint) vs ranked DISCRIMINATORS (implementable-from-text > separability > tokens-without-a-build-fight > DO-deployable, which has near-zero discriminating power and is recorded as such), combined LEXICOGRAPHICALLY rather than by weighted score — invented weights are unfalsifiable and hide which criterion actually decided, and a lexicographic rule makes the decisive criterion nameable, which is what a reversal clause needs. Ties go to the incumbent, declared in advance so a challenger must WIN a discriminator rather than merely match. Candidate rule: exactly 3, varying ONE AXIS AT A TIME (dependency policy; rendering model) so the outcome is attributable to an axis rather than a brand, with the fourth cell excluded-with-reason in the style of the capability table's OUT rows. No technologies are named in this plan, on purpose — same reason AS-31 named the slot and no candidates.

SPIKE: yes, warranted, and narrow. One screen — the invoice create/edit server half (repeating line-item group, server-side field-level validation, tokens.css, one stubbed Stripe call behind a module boundary) — built in each surviving candidate. Six measurements including gate (c) executed with egress blocked, and cold-error legibility (introduce one typo, record verbatim what the implementer sees). An IC who cannot see the error cannot debug and has nobody to ask. Gates first, eliminate, spike only survivors. Scratchpad only, fresh directory per candidate, nothing committed — a stray apps/ spike dir would be permanently un-cleanable under the shared-worktree rule. $0. One-tick box; on expiry, publish with gaps labeled and proceed.

CHAT APP: evidence, not precedent. It genuinely evidences that agent ICs can build and MAINTAIN a zero-dependency Node app under compose across 25+ merged tasks. It does not reach: no third-party integration (so the SDK-vs-hand-rolled question, which interacts with the custody chokepoint, is untested), no untrusted users (CSRF/sessions/cookie flags/escaping are what frameworks give free and hand-rolled code gets wrong — the strongest argument against extrapolating it), and public/app.js is 46,868 bytes in ONE hand-rolled file, 66%% of its front-end JS — a warning, not a template, and the doc must PROJECT that size for 7 screens x ~5 states rather than hand-wave it.

TIME-BOX: one tick for the whole task, spike included. AS-36 is spine task 1 with fourteen tasks behind it; a decision with a labeled gap beats no decision, because the reversal triggers make it recoverable. No branch, no worktree — documents and .lattice only, direct to master, no push (plan section 13). Reviewer should start with plan section 11.1: read criteria and evidence, STOP before the recommendation, write your own ranking, then compare.

DECISION LANDED: docs/engineering/01-stack-decision.md (980 lines, commit 58b1c3c). No branch/worktree per plan §13 — documents only.

RECOMMENDATION: build apps/invoicing in the C2 shape — server-rendered Node, small deliberate dependency budget. Node 24 · Express 5 (MIT) · EJS 6 (Apache-2.0), one template per screen · hand-rolled validation · node --test · docker compose with a network_mode:none test service · node:sqlite · hand-rolled Stripe client. Net adopted footprint: 2 direct packages.

RANKING C2 > C1 > C3. DECISIVE CRITERION: discriminator (a), implementable from text alone — specifically the IC context cost measurement (bytes an implementer must read to add one field): C2 18,076 · C1 28,029 · C3 36,812. Lexicographic ordering stopped at discriminator 1; (h)/(g)/(f) corroborate but did not decide.

GATES: all four adjudicated on executed evidence; NO eliminations. (b) compose config valid ×3. (c) suites re-run by me under --network none: exit 0, 5/5 each, 784ms/1941ms/1464ms — instrument validated first with both controls (EAI_AGAIN blocked, status 200 with network). (d) full transitive licence scan. (e) mutation-tested: ban removed -> suite red, restored -> green.

SPIKE (same invoice create/edit screen, 3 fresh scratchpad dirs, nothing committed):
· hand-written lines 937 / 927 / 1,563 — C1 and C2 within 1%, falsifying 'zero deps costs much more code'
· packages 0 / 67 / 30 · disk 0 / 12MB / 366MB · image delta +0 / +11 / +471 MB
· M5 cold-error legibility REVERSED on re-measurement: C1 and C2 suites CATCH the injected typo (4 pass/1 fail); C3's passes 5/5 green — its form is a client component node --test never renders. C3's tsc gives the best message but only if typecheck is in the loop.
· M6 tokens.css byte-identical (12,199) in C1/C2; C3 rewrites it to 7,224 and injects --lightningcss-* properties — criterion (g) failure.

Q1 CLOSED — hand-rolled Stripe client, not the SDK. Decided on (e) surface-to-ban. Executed probe: the SDK emitted the forbidden shape (transfer_data[destination], no Stripe-Account header) unchallenged, and a rogue 'new Stripe()' bypassed the wrapper entirely, so the SDK needs a parameter ban PLUS a source-level import ban. Hand-rolled builder 22 lines blocks both at the wire; webhook verification 11 lines with node:crypto, all three failure modes caught offline. NOTE: the SDK measured 1 direct / 0 transitive deps — that killed my own footprint argument against it, so Q1 rests on enforceability alone.

Q2 CLOSED — node:sqlite. Executed: Postgres reachable on a docker network but 'CANNOT reach: EAI_AGAIN' under --network none; sqlite runs with zero networking. Postgres does NOT fail gate (c) as worded (a bridge is not egress) — SQLite simply satisfies the strongest form, making the gate a one-word proof. AS-39 keeps SQL behind a data-access module; money as integer minor units + currency column (row C-32).

ZOD REJECTED from C2's assigned representative by the dependency policy's own rule 1: 150 lines/5,244B vs 124 lines/3,914B hand-rolled — it ADDED code.

PHASE C AMENDMENT LANDED verbatim in docs/design/00-frontend-design-plan.md, original sentence quoted not deleted.

DIVERGENCES / DEFECTS, all recorded in the doc's amendment log rows 5-7:
1. The plan's §3 amendment text cites '§4.4 of this very plan'; that document HAS no §4.4. Applied verbatim anyway because criterion 10 checks for exactly that wording and silently fixing a citation inside a verbatim block defeats the check. Correct target is milestone plan §8.1. FLAGGING AS A PLAN DEFECT.
2. Gate ordering: (d) pre-screened from registry metadata before any spike existed (eliminated nobody); (b)/(c)/(e) need a runnable artifact for executed evidence so were adjudicated post-build. Outcome identical.
3. Spike model substituted after all three launches failed on a rate limit before starting — same substitute for all three, comparison unaffected.
4. Self-check found and fixed: I claimed app.js was the largest file in the company; it is the largest APPLICATION source file (two docs files are bigger). Corrected.

SELF-CHECK: blind re-derivation run before hand-off — a fresh reviewer given the doc truncated before §10 independently returned C2 > C1 > C3 on criterion (a) via M4, matching the recommendation it had not read. It found 6 defects, all fixed: no threshold for 'genuinely tied' (now defined, with the after-the-fact weakness admitted), (h) adjudicated in adjectives (now measured: framework-touching files C2 1 / C1 2 / C3 7), (a)'s sub-measures had no combination rule (now lexicographic), friction tallies unlabelled, 4 unbacked superlatives, 2 arithmetic slips.

FOR QA (§11 protocol): do the blind re-derivation FIRST, before reading §10. Then the number audit — every comparative adjective must have a number. The two calls most worth challenging: (1) whether a 35% M4 gap really clears 'genuinely tied', since if it does not, the pre-declared tie-break hands this to C1; (2) whether supply-chain footprint (0 vs 67 packages) SHOULD have been a discriminator — under the criteria fixed in advance it is only a gate, and I deliberately did not let it back in after seeing results. That is a criteria-level amendment if the company disagrees.

Status transition and push left to the orchestrator.

REVIEW (AS-36, stack decision) — VERDICT: PASS. 12/12 acceptance criteria met. One inline fix applied and committed (6eb1ed0). No blocking findings. Nine non-blocking findings below, sorted; three are worth backlog tasks.

=== 1. BLIND RE-DERIVATION (plan section 11.1) — RUN FIRST, AND ITS LIMIT DISCLOSED ===

Method: read doc sections 1-7 (criteria, candidates, chat-app argument, gate adjudication, spike, complete matrix), stopped at line 601, wrote my ranking, then read sections 8-13 and the CTO's lattice comment.

MY RANKING: C2 > C1 > C3. Matches section 10.

What decided it FOR ME, in the order the lexicographic rule forced:
- C3 placed last at discriminator (a), sub-measure M5: its suite reports 5/5 green with a live bug. Under a rule that reads M5 first, that ends C3 before M4 or M1 are consulted. It also loses (g) outright and (h) 7-files-to-1, but those are corroboration; the rule never reached them.
- C2 over C1 at discriminator (a), sub-measure M4: 18,076 B vs 28,029 B to change one field, a 35.5% gap, with M5 identical and M1 a 1% dead heat above it. Recomputed: (28029-18076)/28029 = 35.5%.
- I also checked the ranking is not an artifact of the doc's sub-measure ORDER. Of the plausible reorderings of (a)'s sub-measures, only one flips C1/C2 — promoting the friction-log tallies (C1 1 item, C2 2). Section 2.2 excludes those as self-reported, which is consistent with section 6.3 confound 4 and with section 5.3 (where an independent scan overrode an implementer's own licence report). The exclusion runs AGAINST the recommendation's own candidate, so it is not self-serving. Ordering holds.

DISCLOSURE, because it bears on how much this test is worth: my tasking message stated the recommendation (C2), the ranking, and the three M4 byte counts before I opened a file. So my re-derivation was ANCHORED, not blind. I could not un-read it. What survives that contamination is the arithmetic and the counterfactual check above — I verified the stated rule mechanically forces C2 and that no principled reordering flips it — but treat my match as weaker corroboration than the pre-hand-off blind check recorded in amendment-log row 7. If the company wants this protocol step to keep its value, the QA tasking message must not carry the answer. That is a process finding against the tick, not against this document.

=== 2. THE THREE CONTESTED CALLS ===

CALL 1 — does a 35% M4 gap clear "genuinely tied"? YES, and the recommendation does not depend on the threshold.
The 10%-or-opposite-directions definition is admittedly post-hoc and section 2.2 says so in the same breath, which is the right disclosure. The test for reverse-engineering is whether a differently chosen, still-principled threshold flips the result: it would have to sit above 35% to make C1/C2 tied and fire the incumbent tie-break. "Tied unless one candidate differs by more than a third" is not a rule anyone writes in advance for a metric the document itself calls the most direct measure of how much must be read. So the threshold is loose across its whole plausible range and does not carry the decision.
Sharper point, and this is the actual finding: the 10% number NEVER FIRES anywhere in the document. M1 (1%) and M5 (identical) are ties by inspection; M4 (35%) is a difference by inspection. The threshold changed no cell. That is simultaneously why it is not laundering and why its lateness is forgivable.
FINDING 1 (non-blocking, one sentence to fix): the doc discloses the THRESHOLD as defined-after-the-data but gives no such disclosure to the SUB-MEASURE ORDERING inside (a) — M5, then M4, then M1, then the qualitative call, friction logs excluded. Section 2.2 says "their order, fixed here", which is accurate but not flagged as a weakness. That ordering is MORE load-bearing than the threshold: M5-first is what eliminates C3 immediately. Both came from the same pre-hand-off self-check (amendment row 7, items i and iii), so the asymmetry is an oversight, not concealment. Recommend the ordering carry the same admission the threshold carries.

CALL 2 — should supply-chain footprint discriminate? NO. Excluding it is procedurally correct, and the disposal in section 10.2 is the strongest available. But it under-states one thing.
The seven criteria were fixed in AS-36's own description (I re-read it: (a)-(g), "evaluates each against all seven criteria above"). Footprint is not among them; it lives inside gate (d) as cost and licence. Admitting a ninth criterion after seeing 0-vs-67 is exactly the post-hoc reweighting section 2.2 refuses — and it would be laundering in the incumbent's favour, which is no better. Section 10.2 names the number, prices it (+0 vs +11 MB image, 12 MB disk), declines to reweight, and routes the disagreement to a criteria-level amendment. That is not burying it.
FINDING 2 (non-blocking, worth a backlog task): the doc's own evidence shows transitive footprint carrying a GATE-(d)-relevant risk that nothing re-checks. Section 5.3 caught two LGPL-3.0-or-later packages in C3 that its implementer had reported as MIT — i.e. the tree is exactly where a licence problem hides. Section 11 rule 4 and trigger T4 handle FUTURE dependencies, but nothing re-runs the transitive scan over the 60-plus packages already admitted when Express or EJS is upgraded. Suggest T4's observable gain a clause: on any dependency upgrade, re-run the transitive licence scan. This is a standing gate-(d) re-exposure, not a discriminator.
FINDING 3 (non-blocking, small and checkable): the adopted footprint is never stated as a package count. Section 10.3 says removing Zod takes 1 package and 7.7 MB off the measured tree, and section 10.1/12 say "2 direct packages" — but the transitive count for the thing actually being adopted (Express 5 + EJS 6, no Zod) appears nowhere. 67 is the count for a candidate that was not recommended. That is the number a future reader will want, and section 11 rule 4 demands it be counted rather than assumed.

CALL 3 — applying a known-defective citation verbatim. WRONG CALL, right instinct, trivial fix, FIXED INLINE.
Criterion 10's text is: the design plan "carries section 3's wording, dated and attributed. Mechanical: grep for the amendment header." The check is for the amendment HEADER. Correcting a cross-reference would not have defeated it, so the stated reason ("criterion 10 checks for exactly that wording") over-reads the criterion.
The cost lands on a reader, not the author: docs/design/00-frontend-design-plan.md now points at a section of itself that does not exist, and amendment-log row 6 — which explains it — lives in a DIFFERENT document that a reader of the design plan never opens.
The verbatim instinct is right in general. The correct move was to apply verbatim AND leave a visible dated correction in the same file, so the wrong pointer and its correction travel together. Done, inline (see section 4). I also found a SECOND dangling reference in the same block that nobody had flagged: "01-stack-decision.md section (reversal)" — a forward reference written before that document existed. It resolves to section 9 / trigger T1.

=== 3. REPRODUCIBILITY — THE SPIKE HYGIENE vs REVIEWABILITY TENSION, ADJUDICATED ===

WHAT I VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY (ran, did not read):
(i) Every repo-checkable number in section 4 and M6 — re-measured from the working tree, 11 of 11 EXACT: chat total JS 9,920 lines; 17 test files; 0 direct deps (dependencies and devDependencies both absent); no node_modules; public/app.js 46,868 B / 1,197 lines; front-end JS 71,457 B; store.js 36,572 B; style-reference/index.html 84,362 B; tokens.test.mjs 75,613 B; tokens.css 12,199 B.
(ii) Arithmetic — recomputed roughly fifteen derived figures, all correct: M4 gap 35.5%; M1 +66.8% and +68.6% (stated +67/+69); licence spreads summing to exactly 67 and 30; image deltas +11 and +471; 30x disk and 43x image delta; app.js at 65.6% of front-end JS; the 4,261 B per-surface figure and the 149,125 B / 3,809-line projection (computed unrounded, correct); 3.2x app.js, 4.1x store.js, 1.8x style-reference; Zod +21% lines / +34% bytes.
(iii) M5 — the claim I was asked to press, and the one this company has repeatedly found wrong when checked. The artifacts are gone, so I rebuilt the MECHANISM at both ends from the doc's description alone, zero dependencies, Node v24.13.1:
    - C3 shape: a .ts test file containing a genuine TS2551 (row.descrption against a RowState type, no cast, no suppression) whose tests assert against the route handler's return value rather than a rendered component. Result: 5 tests, 5 pass, EXIT 0. Node strips the types without checking them, exactly as claimed.
    - C1/C2 shape: the same typo as a property access inside a server-rendered template (yielding undefined -> empty string, not a throw — matching the doc's "renders value empty" observation), with a behavioural test asserting submitted values are re-rendered. Result: 4 pass, 1 fail, EXIT 1, and the failing test is the round-trip assertion — the same failure the doc reports.
    CONFIRMED: the structural claim is real and reproduces. A client-rendered stack whose tests assert on handler output cannot see a template typo, and type-stripping means the type error does not fail the run either.
    NOT VERIFIED, stated so I do not imply more: (a) the tsc --noEmit half — tsc is not installed and installing it is a network call I will not make, so the TS2551 message quoted in the doc is unverified as an execution, though its error code and "did you mean" form are the correct ones for that defect; (b) that the actual C3 spike's tests were structured the way the doc describes — the artifact is gone, so I verified that the described shape behaves as described, not that the artifact had that shape.
(iv) Scope and constraints — git diff 9f4c822..HEAD touches exactly four paths: the two docs and two .lattice files. No application code. No committed spike artifacts. apps/ contains only chat. Constraint grep (licence/subscription/signup/account/paid/billed/$) returns hits only inside gate definitions, policy rules, or explicit-exclusion contexts; the only "billed" is the argument AGAINST managed Postgres. Nothing recommended costs money or needs an account.

WHAT CANNOT BE REPRODUCED: all six measurements for all three candidates, plus the section 8.1 chokepoint probe and the section 8.2 Postgres/SQLite probe. Artifacts were scratchpad-only per plan sections 7.4 and 13 and are gone. Grading the METHOD as documented, which is the question that matters:
  - M3 gate (c): WELL SPECIFIED. Exact docker run commands, exit codes, counts, runtimes, and — this is the part usually missing — the instrument validated with BOTH controls before use (fetch fails EAI_AGAIN under --network none; the identical probe with networking returns 200). Method recorded, not just outcome.
  - M5: WELL SPECIFIED. Specified well enough that I reproduced both ends from prose alone. Verbatim outputs given for all three.
  - M6: WELL SPECIFIED. Mechanism, byte counts, the injected lightningcss custom properties, the content-hashed filename, and the Content-Length to verify.
  - Gate (e): WELL SPECIFIED as method — mutation-tested (ban commented out, suite re-run, guard restored, suite re-run), with which suites went red per candidate. This is method, not outcome.
  - M2: ADEQUATE. "Walking installed package.json files, one method for all three", and section 11 rule 4 gives a concrete command. Not runnable offline, but re-derivable.
  - M1: UNDER-SPECIFIED. "Recounted from each MANIFEST.tsv" — the manifests are not committed, so the classification rule (which files count as server vs client vs config vs test) is unrecoverable. A re-runner would have to invent it.
  - M4: UNDER-SPECIFIED, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT DECIDED. The task is specified precisely (add client_address_line1, validated, field-level errors, carried to the read-only view) — good. But the inputs are not published: only the totals (5 / 5 / 11 files; 28,029 / 18,076 / 36,812 bytes). The three file lists with per-file byte counts would have cost about fifteen lines and would have made the single decisive number in the document auditable by a reader who cannot rebuild the spikes. This is the gap I would most want closed.

FINDING 4 (non-blocking, worth a backlog task) — MY ADJUDICATION OF THE TENSION, since nobody has ruled: the no-commit rule should STAND. A stray apps/ spike directory is permanently un-cleanable under the shared-worktree rule, and committing three throwaway applications to master to support one decision is worse than the problem it solves. But "do not commit the ARTIFACT" does not entail "do not commit the EVIDENCE." A spike's measurement INPUTS — the M4 file lists, M1's manifest classification, verbatim command transcripts — are small, textual, and belong in the decision document or in notes/<task_id>.md, where they cost nothing and make the numbers auditable after the scratchpad is gone. Recommend that as a standing rule for future spikes. It does not block here: criterion 6 as written asks for numbers with their method, and every number I could check was exact, which is the strongest available proxy for the ones I could not.

=== 4. INLINE FIX APPLIED AND COMMITTED (6eb1ed0) ===
docs/design/00-frontend-design-plan.md. The amendment blockquote is left BYTE-IDENTICAL — acceptance criterion 10's grep still passes (header present), the original Phase C sentence is still quoted rather than deleted, and the string "section 4.4 of this very plan" is still present in the verbatim block. A dated, attributed correction note is APPENDED beneath the block resolving both dangling pointers: "section 4.4 of this very plan" -> docs/engineering/00-d1-v1-milestone-plan.md section 8.1 (verified: it is "Shape: spine -> fan -> join", and it does carry the spine-gates-the-fan argument and the ready-queue invariant the citation was reaching for); and "01-stack-decision.md section (reversal)" -> section 9, trigger T1. Verbatim record preserved, audit trail intact, reader no longer sent to a section that does not exist. Typo-class, no behaviour changed.

=== 5. REMAINING NON-BLOCKING FINDINGS ===
FINDING 5 — the recommended C2 is NOT the measured C2, and the doc never says whether the decisive number survives. C2 was spiked as Express + EJS + Zod; section 10.3 then rejects Zod. Section 10.3 adjusts M2 (minus 1 package, minus 7.7 MB) but says nothing about M1 or M4. I did the arithmetic from the doc's own figures: substituting C1's hand-rolled validator (124 lines / 3,914 B) for Zod's (150 lines / 5,244 B) moves C2's hand-written total 927 -> 901 lines (now BELOW C1's 937) and, if the schema file is one of C2's five files-to-open, M4 18,076 -> 16,746 B, widening C2's lead from 35% to about 40%. So the substitution moves BOTH decisive measures in the winner's favour and the conclusion is untouched — but a reader should not have to derive that. One sentence in section 10.3 closes it. Note the second-order effect that does not flip anything: hand-rolling validation shifts C2's "mostly conventional" characterisation slightly toward bespoke, and that sub-measure ranks fourth, below the M4 that already settled it.
FINDING 6 — the section 4.2 projection's divisor has no stated counting method. "11 distinct render surfaces" is the denominator of 46,868/11 = 4,261, which drives the 149 KB / 3,809-line projection, which justifies section 10.4 item 1 and trigger T7. Criterion 6 requires numbers to carry their method; this one does not. I get 5 by counting "function render*" and 12 by a looser render/open/show/update rule, so 11 is plausible but I cannot reproduce it exactly. The conclusion is robust — at divisor 5 the projection is far worse, and even at 20 it is still 1.75x app.js — so this is a documentation defect, not a numerical one.
FINDING 7 — cold-read test (protocol step 9), the two questions I would have had to ask as AS-37's implementer. (a) Section 10.4 item 6 and section 12 both MANDATE exact-version pins and neither NAMES them. "Express 5" and "EJS 6" are ranges, and the doc's own section 10.3 corpus-drift finding (Zod v4 installed against v3 documentation) is the precise argument for recording the versions actually evaluated. The implementer must pin versions this decision never measured. (b) tokens.css is to be served "byte-identical, no copy, no transform, no hash" but lives at docs/design/tokens/tokens.css, outside apps/invoicing/; in a container it has to enter the image somehow, and "no copy" reads as forbidding the obvious move. C2's spike used sendFile from the project root, which implies a build context wider than the app directory — worth one line. Neither is a blocker; both are one line each, and section 12's claim that "everything needed is above" is very slightly overstated.
